title: S&P 500 Futures Drop, South Korea Kospi Plummets 7% Ahead of U.S. Economic Data – Live Updates
body:
Wall Street opened on a cautious note Thursday, with the S&P 500 futures slipping as investors braced for a wave of U.S. economic releases and corporate earnings, while Asian markets showed a stark contrast: South Korea’s Kospi tumbled nearly 7 % after a series of disappointing corporate reports and heightened concerns over a slowing domestic economy. The mixed global sentiment underscored the fragile balance between optimism for technology‑driven growth and the reality of tightening monetary conditions.

In the United States, the Nasdaq‑100 futures plunged sharply after a series of tech giants disclosed earnings that fell short of analysts’ expectations. The primary worry among market participants is that many of these firms have been allocating substantial capital to artificial‑intelligence initiatives without a clear path to profitability. Companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft and Alphabet have all reported higher‑than‑expected spending on AI research and infrastructure, prompting investors to question whether the current hype can translate into sustainable earnings. The sell‑off in the Nasdaq‑100 futures was the most pronounced among the major indices, pulling the broader S&P 500 futures down by roughly 0.6 % in early trading.

The downward pressure on U.S. markets was amplified by the looming release of key economic data later in the day, including the consumer price index (CPI) and the weekly jobless claims report. Analysts anticipate that the CPI could reveal persistent inflationary pressures, which would likely reinforce the Federal Reserve’s commitment to maintaining higher interest rates for longer than previously projected. Meanwhile, a weaker-than-expected jobs report could signal a deceleration in the labor market, adding another layer of uncertainty for equity investors. Together, these data points are expected to shape the tone of the market for the remainder of the week and could set the stage for a more defensive positioning across sectors.

Across the Pacific, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index suffered a dramatic 7 % decline, its steepest single‑day drop in over a year. The plunge was triggered by a string of earnings misses from heavyweight conglomerates, most notably Samsung Electronics, whose profit margin contracted amid rising component costs and a slowdown in smartphone demand. In addition, the Korean government’s recent decision to delay certain fiscal stimulus measures, coupled with a modest rise in the country’s policy rate, has heightened investor anxiety about domestic consumption and export growth. The market reaction was further exacerbated by a weaker won, which has increased the cost of imported raw materials for manufacturers and eroded profit forecasts for export‑oriented firms.

The divergent movements between U.S. and Korean markets illustrate a broader theme: investors are increasingly scrutinizing the sustainability of growth narratives that hinge on emerging technologies and fiscal support. In the United States, the AI boom has spurred a wave of capital expenditures that many analysts deem premature, especially as the sector grapples with a shortage of proven revenue models. Conversely, South Korea’s reliance on traditional manufacturing and electronics exports makes it more vulnerable to global supply‑chain disruptions and currency fluctuations. Both regions are therefore navigating a delicate equilibrium between innovation‑driven optimism and the practical constraints of macroeconomic headwinds.

Looking ahead, market participants will be closely watching the upcoming economic releases for clues about the trajectory of inflation and employment. A hotter CPI reading could reinforce expectations of a tighter monetary stance, potentially extending the period of market volatility. Meanwhile, the earnings season is far from over; the performance of mid‑cap tech firms and consumer discretionary companies will be pivotal in determining whether the current sell‑off is a temporary correction or the beginning of a more prolonged pullback. In Asia, the Kospi’s recovery will likely depend on whether the Korean government can deliver timely policy support and whether key exporters can stabilize margins amid a volatile global demand environment. The next few weeks will therefore be critical in shaping investor confidence across both continents, as they weigh the promise of AI‑driven growth against the realities of an uncertain economic landscape.
